You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.

# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.

payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the source paper visibly stuffed inside the source cup in the edited image?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited image shows the paper from the source image placed inside the cup from the source image, with visible evidence it has been stuffed into it. Fail if the matched paper and cup are assessable and the paper is visibly outside the cup or only resting nearby or on its rim. Unknown if the source objects cannot be reliably matched in the edited image, or their relationship cannot be assessed.
node.binding: Identify the requested paper and cup by their visual and contextual roles in the source image, allowing their appearance to change in the edited image. Judge whether that paper is stuffed inside that cup; do not require exact color or shape matches.

node_traces.evidence: The source paper and cup are visible, but the edited image shows a hand holding a blue printed item near a round object. The source paper and cup cannot be reliably matched to these objects, so whether the paper was stuffed into the cup cannot be established.

fulfillment: The node’s binding is too vague to preserve object identity across the source and edited images. The trace says the source white paper and blue cup cannot be reliably matched to the edited blue printed item and round object, yet support 2 treats them as matched and credits partial progress. Tighten the binding/criteria to require evidence that the edited objects are the same paper and cup, and that the paper has actually moved toward or into that cup; do not infer progress from merely nearby objects. Keep completion distinct from partial progress: paper on or near the rim is not proof it is stuffed inside. When identity or placement is genuinely unresolved, retain unknown rather than forcing a label. The reference ‘no’ constrains the aggregate but is not atomic evidence; investigate the conflicting support judgments rather than encoding ‘no’ as the answer. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported, so focus the repair on binding and evidence consistency.
s2: Repair the binding so it identifies the source paper and cup by their visible attributes and requires reliable cross-image identity, not merely objects with similar roles. Here the source has a white sheet and a blue cup; the edited image shows a blue printed item and a round reddish object. The trace’s claim that these are matched—and that the paper is partly in the cup—is not supported by the images. Do not count proximity or an apparent paper-like shape as progress without evidence that it is the same paper being placed toward the same cup. Keep the node’s partial-progress criterion distinct from completion, and return unknown when identity or placement cannot be assessed. Treat the aggregate “no” as a constraint to investigate, not as atomic ground truth or a reason to force a negative. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated; focus the structural edit on binding and evidence thresholds.
